en: The Shorter Exposition:
The Exposition of the Chapter on the Way to the Far Shore;
The Exposition of the Questions.
3. The Exposition of the Questions of the Young Brahmin Puṇṇaka "O you who see the root of the imperturbable," [said the Venerable Puṇṇaka].
I have come with a question:
On what do the seers, men,
khattiyas, and brahmins depend upon the deities?
Many have performed sacrifices here in the world;
I ask you, Blessed One, explain this to me:
"The seer of the root is the unshaken one"—here, "shaking" (ejā) is said to be craving (taṇhā).

Whatever lust, infatuation, ... [as above] ... covetousness, greed, the unwholesome root—this is the agitation, this is the craving, which has been abandoned by the Buddha, the Blessed One; it is cut off at the root, made like a palm stump, obliterated so that it is no more subject to future arising.
Therefore the Buddha is "unagitated.
Because of the abandoning of agitation, he is unagitated.
The Blessed One does not waver in gain, nor does he waver in loss; he does not waver in fame, nor does he waver in disrepute;
he does not waver in praise, nor does he waver in blame; he does not waver in pleasure, nor does he waver in pain—he does not move, does not shake, does not tremble, and does not quiver.
"Unshaken.

"One who sees the root," said the Blessed One, "is one who sees the cause, sees the source, sees the origin, sees the arising, sees the provenance, sees the manifestation, sees the nutriment, sees the object, sees the condition, and sees the origination.
There are three unwholesome roots:"
Greed is a root of unwholesomeness, hatred is a root of unwholesomeness, and delusion is a root of unwholesomeness.
For this was said by the Blessed One:
"Bhikkhus, there are these three sources for the origination of kamma."
What are the three?
Greed is a cause for the origination of kamma; hatred is a cause for the origination of kamma; delusion is a cause for the origination of kamma.
Monks, it is not through kamma born of greed, kamma born of hatred, or kamma born of delusion that gods are known, nor humans, nor any other happy destinies whatsoever.
Then, monks, through action born of greed, action born of hatred, and action born of delusion, hell is made known;

the animal realm is made known; the sphere of hungry ghosts is made known; or whatever other miserable destinations there may be for the production of a personal existence in hell, the animal realm, or the sphere of hungry ghosts.
"These are the three unwholesome roots"—thus the Blessed One knows and sees.
In this way, the Blessed One is a seer of the root...
[and so on] ...a seer of the origin.
There are three roots of the wholesome:
the root of the wholesome that is non-greed, the root of the wholesome that is non-hatred, and the root of the wholesome that is non-delusion.
For this was said by the Blessed One:

“Monks, these three … [as above] … Monks, hell is not known through action born of non-greed, action born of non-hatred, and action born of non-delusion; the animal realm is not known; the sphere of hungry ghosts is not known; nor indeed are any other miserable destinies known.
Rather, monks, through action born of non-greed, action born of non-hatred, and action born of non-delusion, the devas [are known].”
“Human beings are discerned, and whatever other happy destinations there may be— whether among devas or humans—
as well as the manifestation of individual existence therein.
“The Blessed One knows and sees these three roots of the wholesome.”
In this way, the Blessed One is one who sees the root...
[and so on] ...he is one who sees the origin.
For this was said by the Blessed One:

“Bhikkhus, whatever states are unwholesome, partaking of the unwholesome, belonging to the side of the unwholesome—all these have ignorance as their root, converge upon ignorance, and are rooted out by the eradication of ignorance.
The Blessed One knows and sees that all these go to their eradication.
In this way, the Blessed One is a seer of the root... [and so on].
One who sees the origin [of suffering].
For this was said by the Blessed One:
“Bhikkhus, whatever states are wholesome, partaking of the wholesome, belonging to the side of the wholesome—all these have heedfulness as their root and converge upon heedfulness.”
“‘Heedfulness is declared to be the foremost of those qualities’—thus the Blessed One knows and sees.
In this way, the Blessed One is one who sees the root... [and so on] ...he is one who sees the origin.”
Or rather, the Blessed One knows and sees:
"Ignorance is the root of volitional formations; volitional formations are the root of consciousness; consciousness is the root of name-and-form;
name-and-form is the root of the six sense bases; the six sense bases are the root of contact; contact is the root of feeling."
“Feeling is the root of craving; craving is the root of clinging; clinging is the root of existence;
existence is the root of birth; birth is the root of aging and death”—thus the Blessed One knows and sees.
In this way, the Blessed One is a seer of the root...
[and so on] ...a seer of the origin.
Or rather, the Blessed One knows and sees.

“The eye is the root of eye-diseases; the ear is the root of ear-diseases; the nose is the root of nose-diseases; the tongue is the root of tongue-diseases; the body is the root of body-diseases; the mind is the root of mental sufferings”—thus the Blessed One knows and sees.

In this way, the Blessed One is a seer of the root, a seer of the cause, a seer of the source, a seer of the origin, a seer of the genesis, a seer of the arising, a seer of the nutriment, a seer of the object, a seer of the condition, and a seer of the origination.
"Unshaken, seeing the root.
Thus, "the Venerable Puṇṇaka"—this is the grammatical connection of the words... [etc.
...the Venerable Puṇṇaka.

"There is coming for the sake of a question; I have come seeking a question; I have come desiring to ask a question; I have come desiring to hear a question"—thus too there is coming for the sake of a question.

Or alternatively, there is the coming, the approaching, the drawing near, the arrival, and the attendance of those who seek a question, who desire to ask a question, and who desire to hear a question. Thus there is coming for the sake of a question.
"In this way too, there is a source for the question.
Or rather, you possess the tradition of the questions; you are capable and competent.
You are able to explain and answer what has been asked by me; you can bear this burden."
Thus there is a source for this question:
"Upon what do the seers (isayo) depend? By what are they supported, stayed upon, clung to, approached, adhered to, and intent?
"Seers" refers to those known as seers—whosoever have gone forth into the seers' renunciation: Ājīvakas, Nigaṇṭhas, matted-hair ascetics, and forest-dwelling ascetics.
"Manuja" means humans are so called—
on what basis are these seers "manuja"?
[They are] khattiyas, brahmins, and deities.
“Khattiyas” refers to those of whatever kind belong to the khattiya caste.
“Brāhmaṇas” refers to those of whatever kind who address others as “bho.
“Deities” refers to the Ājīvaka deities for the followers of the Ājīvakas, the Nigaṇṭha deities for the followers of the Nigaṇṭhas, and the Jaṭila deities for the followers of the Jaṭilas.
The matted-hair ascetics have deities who are matted-hair ascetics; the disciples of the wanderers have deities who are wanderers; the disciples of the Aviruddhakas have deities who are Aviruddhakas;

those who follow the elephant-vow have elephants as their deities; those who follow the horse-vow have horses as their deities; those who follow the cow-vow have cows as their deities; those who follow the dog-vow have dogs as their deities;
those who follow the crow-vow have crows as their deities; and those who follow the Vāsudeva-vow [have deities who are Vāsudevas].
Vāsudeva is the deity for those who worship Vāsudeva; Baladeva is the deity for those who worship Baladeva; Puṇṇabhadda is the deity for those who worship Puṇṇabhadda;
Maṇibhadda is the deity for those who worship Maṇibhadda; Aggī is the deity for those who worship Aggī;

the Nāgas are the deities for those who worship the Nāgas; the Supaṇṇas are the deities for those who worship the Supaṇṇas; the Yakkhas are the deities for those who worship the Yakkhas; and the Asuras are the deities for those who worship the Asuras.

The Asuras are the deities of those who have the Asuras as their presiding deity; the Gandhabbas are the deities of those who have the Gandhabbas as their presiding deity; the Great Kings are the deities of those who have the Great Kings as their presiding deity;
the Moon is the deity of those who have the Moon as their presiding deity; the Sun is the deity of those who have the Sun as their presiding deity;

Indra is the deity of those who have Indra as their presiding deity; Brahmā is the deity of those who have Brahmā as their presiding deity; the Deva is the deity of those who have the Deva as their presiding deity; and the Directions are the deities of those who have the Directions as their presiding deity.
"Those who are worthy of offerings are their deities"—this refers to the khattiyas and brahmins as the deities of others.
"In this world, many performed sacrifices"—here, 'sacrifice' (yañña) refers to the articles to be given: robes, almsfood, lodgings, and medicinal requisites for the sick.
"Food, drink, clothing, vehicles, garlands, scents, ointments, beds, dwellings, and lamps.
"They performed sacrifices" means that those who seek, search for, and pursue sacrifice—namely, robes, almsfood, lodgings, and medicinal requisites for the sick;
food, drink, clothing, vehicles, garlands, scents, ointments, beds, dwellings, and lamps—they too perform sacrifice.
Those who prepare a sacrifice—robes, almsfood, lodgings, and medicinal requisites for the sick; food and drink...
[and so on] ...beds, dwellings, and lamps—they too make that sacrifice possible.
Those who give a sacrifice, offer it, and relinquish it—robes, almsfood, lodgings, and medicinal requisites for the sick; food and drink... [and so on] ...they too make that sacrifice possible.
They provide beds, dwellings, and lighting; they too perform sacrifices.
"Many" means either these sacrifices are many, or these sacrificers and priests are many, or these recipients of offerings are many.
How are these sacrifices many?

These sacrifices are for many people: robes, almsfood, lodgings, and medicinal requisites for the sick; food, drink, clothing, vehicles, garlands, scents, ointments, beds, dwellings, and lamps—thus these sacrifices are manifold.
And how are the sacrificers and priests manifold?
These sacrificers are many: khattiyas, brahmins, vessas, suddas, householders, renunciants, gods, and humans—in this way, these sacrificers are numerous.
How are these worthy recipients of offerings numerous?
"These many worthy recipients of offerings—numerous ascetics and brahmins, the poor, the wretched, the vagrants, and beggars—thus these worthy recipients are numerous.
'In this world' means in the human world; there they performed sacrifices."
"O Blessed One, I ask you; tell me this:
'I ask' refers to three kinds of questions."

There is a question for the purpose of illuminating what has not been seen, a question for the purpose of correlating what has been seen, and a question for the purpose of cutting through doubt. What is the question for the purpose of illuminating what has not been seen?

It is when the characteristic of a thing is, by its very nature, unknown, unseen, unmeasured, uninvestigated, unmanifested, and unclarified; one asks a question for the sake of knowing it, seeing it, measuring it, investigating it, making it manifest, and clarifying it.
This is a question for the purpose of revealing what has not been seen.
What is a question for the purpose of correlating what has been seen?
It is when the characteristic is known by nature—seen, weighed, judged, made manifest, and fully clarified.
He asks a question for the purpose of comparing views with other wise people—
this is a question for the purpose of comparing what has been seen.
What is a question for the purpose of cutting through doubt?
By nature he is prone to doubt, prone to perplexity, and full of uncertainty, thinking:
"Is it thus? Is it not thus? What is it? How is it? He asks a question for the purpose of cutting through his doubt.
This is the question for cutting through doubt.
These are the three questions.
There are another three questions:
Questions asked by humans, questions asked by non-humans, and questions asked by a created being.
What is a question asked by humans? Humans approach the Buddha, the Blessed One, and ask; monks ask; nuns [ask].
Laymen ask, laywomen ask, kings ask, kshatriyas ask, brahmins ask,
vaishyas ask, shudras ask, householders ask, and those who have gone forth ask—
this is questioning by humans.
What is the question of non-human beings? Non-human beings approach the Buddha, the Blessed One, and ask a question;
nāgas ask, supaṇṇas ask, yakkhas ask, asuras ask, gandhabbas ask, and the Great Kings ask.
Indras ask, Brahmās ask, and deities ask—
this is a question by non-humans.
What is a question by a created being?

When the Blessed One emanates a mind-made form, complete in all its limbs and parts with unimpaired faculties, and that emanation approaches the Buddha, the Blessed One, and asks a question which the Blessed One answers—
this is a "question by an emanation."
These are three questions.
There are another three questions:
a question concerning one’s own welfare, a question concerning the welfare of others, and a question concerning the welfare of both.
There are another three kinds of questions:
a question concerning the welfare pertaining to the present life, a question concerning the welfare pertaining to future lives, and a question concerning the ultimate meaning.
There are yet another three kinds of questions:
An inquiry into blamelessness, an inquiry into the absence of defilement, and an inquiry into purification.
Furthermore, there are three other inquiries:
an inquiry into the past, an inquiry into the future, and an inquiry into the present.
There are another three kinds of questions:
a question about the internal, a question about the external, and a question about both the internal and the external.
There are yet another three kinds of questions:
An inquiry concerning the wholesome, an inquiry concerning the unwholesome, and an inquiry concerning the indeterminate.
There are another three inquiries— an inquiry concerning the aggregates,
an inquiry concerning the elements, and an inquiry concerning the sense bases.
There are another three questions:
the question on the foundations of mindfulness, the question on the right efforts, and the question on the bases of psychic power.
There are yet another three questions—
The inquiry into the faculties, the inquiry into the powers, and the inquiry into the factors of enlightenment.
There are another three inquiries:
the inquiry into the path, the inquiry into the fruit, and the inquiry into Nibbāna.
“I ask you” means: I ask you, I entreat you, I beseech you, I propitiate you, saying “Speak to me,” thus I ask you.
“The Blessed One” (Bhagavā) is a designation for reverence... [and so on] ... it is a realization-designation, namely: the Blessed One.
"Tell me this"—that is: speak it, declare it, teach it, lay it out, establish it, reveal it, analyze it, make it plain, and explain it—"I ask you, Blessed One, tell me this.
Thus that brahmin spoke.
“O seer of the root of the unshaken one,” said the Venerable Puṇṇaka,
“I have come with a question.”
Upon what did the seers, men,
kshatriyas, brahmins, and deities rely when they performed various sacrifices here in the world?
“I ask you, Blessed One, tell me this.
“Whosoever these seers among men may be,
Puṇṇaka,” said the Blessed One.
Khattiyas and brahmins,
O Puṇṇaka, desiring this very state of existence, have here in the world performed many sacrifices for the gods.
"Those who, overcome by old age, performed sacrifices;
those who were these seers among men"—
the phrase "those who were any" (*ye keci*) is a term that encompasses everything in every way, entirely, without exception, exhaustively, and inclusively.
"Whosoever":
"seers" (isayo) refers to those known as seers who have gone forth into the seer's life—the Ājīvakas, the Nigaṇṭhas, the matted-hair ascetics, and the forest-dwelling ascetics.
"Men" (manujā) means they are called human beings.
"Whosoever these seers, humans, Puṇṇakas," said the Blessed One, "Khattiyas, Brāhmaṇas, and deities. Regarding "Khattiyas":
it refers to those of whatever kind belong to the Khattiya caste.
"Brahmins" refers to those who address others as "bho.
"Deities" refers to the Ājīvaka disciples— the Ājīvakas being their deities— and so on, up to the deities of the quarters for the followers of the Disāvatikas.
"Those who are worthy of offerings are their deities"— namely,
for the kṣatriyas and brahmins, the deities are [their deities].
Thus they performed various sacrifices here in the world.
"Sacrifice" (yañña) refers to the objects of giving: robes, almsfood, lodgings, medicinal requisites for the sick, food, drink, ... [and so on] ... beds, dwellings, and lamps.
"They performed sacrifices" means those who seek, search for, and pursue sacrifice ... [and so on] ... beds, dwellings, and lamps—they too perform sacrifice.
"Diverse" means these sacrifices are diverse; or these sacrificers are diverse; or these recipients of offerings are diverse ... [and so on] ... thus these recipients of offerings are diverse.
"In this world" means in the human world; "they performed sacrifices here in many places in the world.
"Hoping for this state of being, Puṇṇaka"—that is, hoping for rebirth in this very existence.
"Longing for" means longing for the acquisition of forms, longing for the acquisition of sounds, longing for the acquisition of odors,
longing for the acquisition of tastes, longing for the acquisition of tangibles,
longing for the acquisition of a son, longing for the acquisition of a wife, longing for the acquisition of wealth, and longing for the acquisition of fame.
Hoping for the attainment of sovereignty; hoping for the attainment of a personal existence in a great khattiya family;
hoping for the attainment of a personal existence in a great brahmin family; hoping for the attainment of a personal existence in a great householder family;
hoping for the attainment of a personal existence among the gods of the Four Great Kings; [hoping for the attainment of a personal existence] among the Tāvatiṃsa gods.
"Among the Yāma devas, the Tusita devas, the Nimmānarati devas, the Paranimmitavasavatti devas,
and the Brahmakāyika devas— expecting, desiring, relishing, longing for, yearning for, and craving the acquisition of a personal existence. Thus it is "expecting."

"Puṇṇaka, ‘this state of being’ (itthattaṃ): here, those who aspire to the production of a personal existence (attabhāvābhinibbatti)—aspiring to the production of a personal existence here in a great khattiya clan...
[and so on] ... aspiring to the production of a personal existence here among the gods of Brahma’s company; those who desire, approve, long for, yearn for, and crave—it is these who are ‘aspiring.
Thus, Puṇṇaka, it is ‘this state of being.’"
"Dependent on aging they performed sacrifices": dependent on aging, dependent on illness, dependent on death, dependent on sorrow, lamentation, pain, grief, and despair.
Whatever they were dependent on birth, that very thing they were dependent on aging;
whatever they were dependent on aging, that very thing they were dependent on illness.
Whatever is for you dependent on illness, that is the same as being dependent on death.
Whatever is for you dependent on death, that is the same as being dependent on sorrow, lamentation, pain, grief, and despair.
Whatever is for you dependent on sorrow, lamentation, pain, grief, and despair, that is the same as being dependent on the various realms of existence.
Whatever is dependent on your destiny is the same as what is dependent on your rebirth.
Whatever is dependent on your rebirth is the same as what is dependent on your relinking.
Whatever is dependent on your relinking is the same as what is dependent on your becoming.
Whatever is dependent on existence for you is precisely what is dependent on saṃsāra for you.
Whatever is dependent on saṃsāra for you is precisely what is dependent on the round, to which they are attached, approached, clinging, and devoted.
Thus, being dependent on aging, they performed sacrifices.
Therefore the Blessed One said:
“Whatever sages there are among these humans,
(‘Puṇṇaka,’ said the Blessed One)”
Khattiyas and brahmins,
O Puṇṇaka, desiring this very state of existence, have here in the world performed many sacrifices for the sake of the deities.
“Those who, overcome by old age, performed sacrifices”—
thus spoke the Venerable Puṇṇaka regarding whatever sages there may be among mankind.
The khattiyas and brahmins here in the world have performed many sacrifices for the sake of the deities;
O Blessed One, were they diligent in the path of sacrifice?
They have crossed over birth and old age, dear sir;
I ask you, Blessed One, tell me this:
who are these seers among mankind?
"Whosoever... [as before] ...
"Has the Blessed One been heedful regarding the path of sacrifice?
"Kaccisu" is a question of doubt, a question of perplexity, a question of uncertainty, a question of indecision.
“Is it thus? Is it not thus? What is it? How is it?”—thus they asked.
“They” refers to those who perform sacrifices and act as priests.
"Bhagavā" is a designation for reverence... [and so on] ...it is a descriptive term based on realization, namely "Bhagavā"—did you hear that from the Blessed One?
"Be heedful on the path of sacrifice": it is sacrifice itself that is called the "path of sacrifice."
Just as the noble path is the way of the noble ones, the path of the gods, the path of Brahmā, and the way of Brahmā, even so the sacrifice itself is called the way of sacrifice.

"Diligent" means: diligent in the way of sacrifice, performing it with care, performing it with persistence, acting with steadfastness, living without shrinking back, not casting off their desire, not casting off their burden, practicing that [sacrifice], being devoted to that, making that their priority, inclining toward that, leaning toward that, and tending toward that.
"Devoted to that, intent on that, with that as their supreme goal"—these too are diligent in the path of sacrifice.
And those who seek, search for, and strive after sacrifice, as well as robes, almsfood, lodgings, and medicinal requisites for the sick; food and drink... [and so forth].
Those who provide beds, dwellings, and lighting with due care...
[and so on] ...being intent upon that, they too are diligent in the path of sacrifice.
And those who prepare sacrifices—robes, almsfood, lodgings, and medicinal requisites for the sick; food and drink... [and so on] ...[they too are diligent in the path of sacrifice].
Those who provide beds, dwellings, and lighting with due care...
[and so on] ...being dominated by that [the Dhamma], they too are diligent in the path of sacrifice.
And those who give a sacrifice, who offer it, who relinquish robes, almsfood, lodgings, medicinal requisites for the sick, food, drink... [and so on].
"Those who provide beds, dwellings, and lighting with due care...
[and] who are dominated by that [virtue]—are they indeed diligent in the path of sacrifice?
May the Blessed One consider whether they are diligent in the path of sacrifice."
“They have crossed over birth and aging, dear sir”—they have crossed over, transcended, leaped across, surmounted, and passed beyond aging-and-death.
“Dear sir” (*mārisa*) is a term of endearment, a term of respect; it is a designation for one who possesses reverence and deference.
“Dear sir, they have crossed over birth and aging.”
"I ask you, Blessed One, tell me. "I ask you" means:
I ask you, I entreat you, I beseech you, I propitiate you;
"tell me"—thus, "I ask you."
"Bhagavā" is a designation for reverence... [and so on] ...it is a descriptive term based on realization—namely, "the Blessed One.
"Tell me" means: speak, declare, teach, describe, establish, reveal, analyze, make plain, and explain.
"I ask you, Blessed One, please tell me this.
Thus that brahmin said:
"Whatever sages there are among these men..."
(Thus spoke the Venerable Puṇṇaka:
"Khattiyas and brahmins have performed sacrifices for the gods here in this world in many ways."
“Were they diligent, O Blessed One, on the path of sacrifice?
Did they, dear sir, cross over birth and old age?
I ask you this, Blessed One; please tell me.”
“They pray, they praise, they invoke, they offer oblations,” said the Blessed One,
“because they crave for sensual pleasures and for gain.”
"Those who are engaged in sacrifice and stained by the passion for existence have not transcended birth and old age; so I say.
They make aspirations, they offer praise, they utter incantations, and they perform oblations."
They aspire: they aspire for the acquisition of forms; they aspire for the acquisition of sounds; they aspire for the acquisition of odors;
they aspire for the acquisition of tastes; they aspire for the acquisition of tangibles; they aspire for the acquisition of sons; they aspire for the acquisition of wives;
they aspire for the acquisition of wealth; they aspire for the acquisition of fame; they aspire for the acquisition of lordship.
They aspire: they aspire to obtain a personal existence in a great khattiya clan; they aspire to obtain a personal existence in a great brahmin clan...

[and so on] ...in a great householder clan; they aspire to obtain a personal existence among the gods of the Four Great Kings... [and so on] ...among the gods of Brahmā’s retinue; they desire, accept, long for, and yearn for this—thus, "they aspire."
"They praise" means they praise the sacrifice, or they praise the fruit, or they praise those worthy of offerings.

How do they praise the sacrifice? "What is pure has been given; what is pleasing has been given; what is excellent has been given; it was given at the right time; it was given as something allowable; it was given with discrimination; it was given blamelessly; it was given repeatedly; by giving, the mind has become serene"—thus they praise the sacrifice.
They praise, extol, laud, and commend it.
This is how they praise the sacrifice.
How do they praise the fruit?
"Because of this cause, there will be the acquisition of form...
[and so on] ...there will be the acquisition of an individual existence among the devas of the Brahma-body"—
thus they praise, extol, laud, and commend it.
Thus they praise the fruit.
How do they praise those worthy of offerings?

Those worthy of offerings are endowed with noble birth, endowed with a noble lineage, reciters of the scriptures, bearers of the mantras, and masters who have reached the further shore of the three Vedas.

They were masters of the *Nighaṇṭu* and *Keṭubha*, of the analysis of syllables, and of the histories as the fifth; they were experts in the *Pada-pāṭha* and *Veyyākaraṇa*, and unerring in the Lokāyata and the marks of a Great Man.
They were either free from lust or practicing for the subduing of lust; free from hatred or practicing for the subduing of hatred;
free from delusion or practicing for the subduing of delusion; and they were endowed with faith, endowed with virtue, and endowed with concentration.
"Endowed with wisdom, endowed with liberation, endowed with the knowledge and vision of liberation"—
thus they praise, extol, laud, and commend them. In this way, they praise those worthy of offerings.
They long for it, they praise it.
"They crave" means they crave the acquisition of forms, they crave the acquisition of sounds, they crave the acquisition of odors, they crave the acquisition of tastes ... [and so on] ...
they crave the acquisition of a personal existence among the devas of the Brahma-body.
“They hope, they praise, they long for;

they sacrifice” means they give, they offer sacrifices, they relinquish—robes, almsfood, lodgings, and medicinal requisites for the sick; food, drink, clothing, vehicles, garlands, scents, unguents, beds, dwellings, and lamps—they hope, they praise, they long for, they sacrifice, O Puṇṇaka, said the Blessed One.
“They crave for sensual pleasures dependent on gain”: dependent on the acquisition of forms, they crave for sensual pleasures;

dependent on the acquisition of sounds, they crave for sensual pleasures … [and so on] … dependent on the acquisition of a personal existence among the devas of the Brahma-group, they crave for and long for sensual pleasures.
Thus, “they crave for sensual pleasures dependent on gain.”
"Those engaged in sacrifice, stained by the lust for existence, have not crossed over birth and aging;
so I say"—here "those" refers to the sacrificers.

"Engaged in sacrifice" means they are joined to, intent upon, devoted to, fully occupied with, and dedicated to sacrifice; they practice it, are habituated to it, hold it dear, are inclined toward it, tend toward it, lean toward it, are resolved upon it, and have it as their dominant concern.
They are engaged in sacrifice;

"stained by the lust for existence" (bhavarāgaratta) means that what is called the lust for existence is the desire for existence, the lust for existence, the delight in existence, the craving for existence, the affection for existence, the fever for existence, the infatuation with existence, and the clinging to existence.
By the lust for existence, they are stained, greedy, infatuated, muddled, clinging, attached, fastened, and obstructed in regard to states of existence.
"Those engaged in sacrifice, stained by passion for existence, have not crossed over birth and aging," so I say.

Those engaged in sacrifice, stained by passion for existence, have not crossed over, have not emerged from, have not leaped over, have not transcended, and have not gone beyond birth, aging, and death; they have not escaped from birth, aging, and death.
"Unreleased, not having transcended, not having fully transcended, and not having passed beyond, they revolve within birth, aging, and death; they revolve within the path of saṃsāra.
Followed by birth, pursued by aging, overcome by sickness, and struck down by death, they are without protection, without shelter, without refuge, and have become without a refuge.
Thus do I speak, I declare, I teach, I make known, I establish, I reveal, I analyze, I make plain, and I illuminate.
“Engaged in sacrifice and devoted to the passion for existence, they have not transcended birth and old age; so I say.
Therefore the Blessed One said:
“They pray, they praise, they invoke, and they offer oblations.”
"O Puṇṇaka," said the Blessed One,
"they long for sensual pleasures depending on gain;
they are devoted to sacrifice and stained by passion for existence."
"I say they have not transcended birth and aging," said the Venerable Puṇṇaka, "if they have not transcended them while engaged in sacrifice."
By means of sacrifices, O dear sir, one [transcends] birth and old age;
but who indeed in the world of gods and men has transcended birth and old age, O dear sir?
I ask you, Blessed One, tell me this:

if those who were engaged in sacrifice—that is, those sacrificers engaged in sacrifice—were stained by the lust for existence, they did not cross over, they did not transcend, they did not leap over, they did not surmount, and they did not pass beyond birth, aging, and death. From birth, aging, and death...
Not having departed, not having escaped, not having transcended, not having surmounted, and not having passed beyond birth, aging, and death, they revolve within birth, aging, and death;
they revolve within the path of saṃsāra.
Followed by birth, pursued by aging, overcome by sickness, struck down by death, without protection, without shelter, without refuge, and having become one who has no refuge—thus [they are].
"And they have not transcended the bonds of sacrifice.
Thus spoke the Venerable Puṇṇaka. "Thus" (*icca*) is a grammatical conjunction (*padasandhi*). ... [etc. ...
The Venerable Puṇṇaka.
"By means of sacrifices, O dear sir, [one overcomes] birth and old age.
Regarding "by means of sacrifices": by means of abundant sacrifices, by means of various sacrifices, by means of manifold sacrifices.
"Sir," this is a term of endearment, a term of respect, a designation used with reverence and deference—"Sir.

"By means of sacrifices, Sir, one crosses over birth and old age"—but who indeed in the world of gods and humans, Sir, has crossed over birth and old age? Who is it in this world together with its gods?
In the world with its gods, Māras, and Brahmās, among this generation with its ascetics and brahmins, its devas and humans, he has crossed over birth, aging, and death;
he has transcended it, surpassed it, overcome it, and gone beyond it.
"Mārisa" is a term of endearment, a term of respect; "Mārisa" is a designation used out of reverence and deference.
"Now then, who in the world of gods and humans has crossed over birth and old age, O Blessed One?
I ask you, speak to me. "I ask you" means:
I ask you, I entreat you, I beseech you, I propitiate you; please tell this to me.
I ask you.
"Bhagavā" is a designation for reverence... [and so forth] ...it is a designation based on realization—that is to say, "Bhagavā."
"Tell me this"— that is, speak it, declare it, teach it, describe it, establish it, reveal it, analyze it, make it plain, and explain it—
"I ask you, Blessed One, tell me this.
That is what that brahmin said.
“If those engaged in sacrifice have not transcended birth and old age through sacrifices, O venerable sir,” said the Venerable Puṇṇaka.
Then who indeed in the world of gods and humans, O Blessed One, has crossed over birth and old age?
I ask you this, Blessed One; please tell me.
"Having discerned the high and low in the world,
O Puṇṇaka," said the Blessed One,
"he for whom there is no agitation anywhere in the world;"
"Saintly, smokeless, untroubled, and free from longing—he has crossed over birth and aging; of him I say this.

"Having reckoned the higher and lower worlds in the world"—by "reckoning" (saṅkhā) is meant knowledge, which is wisdom, understanding... [and so on] ...non-delusion, investigation of phenomena, right view.
"Self and other":
"self" refers to one's own personal existence,
while "other" refers to the personal existence of another.

The near is said to be one's own form, feeling, perception, volitional formations, and consciousness; the far is said to be the form, feeling, perception, volitional formations, and consciousness of another.
The near is said to be the six internal sense bases; the far is said to be the six external sense bases.
The near is said to be the world of human beings; the far is said to be the world of devas.
The near is called the sense-sphere realm (*kāmadhātu*); the far is called the form realm (*rūpadhātu*) and the formless realm (*arūpadhātu*).
Alternatively, the near is called the sense-sphere realm and the form realm; the far is called the formless realm.
Having discerned the near and the far in the world as impermanent, as suffering, as a disease, as a tumor... [and so forth].
"Having understood, weighed, scrutinized, discerned, and made manifest [the world] by way of its escape"—
this is what is meant by "having understood the high and low in the world," O Puṇṇaka,
said the Blessed One.
"Puṇṇaka," said the Blessed One, addressing that brahmin by name.
"Blessed One" (bhagavā) is a term of respect...
[as before] ...namely, "the Blessed One."
"Puṇṇaka," said the Blessed One,
"he for whom there is no wavering anywhere in the world.
"For whom" means for the Arahant whose taints are destroyed.
“Quivering” means quivering due to craving, quivering due to views, quivering due to conceit, quivering due to defilements, and quivering due to sensual desire.
For one in whom these quiverings do not exist—do not exist, are not found, and are not apprehended;

which have been abandoned, cut off, stilled, and subsided, rendered incapable of arising and consumed by the fire of knowledge—[for such a person], “anywhere” means anywhere at all, in anything whatsoever, whether internally, externally, or both internally and externally.
"In the world—the world of the lower realms ... [and so on] ... the world of the sense bases—he who has no wavering anywhere in the world;
he who is peaceful, dustless, free from distress, and without longing, has crossed over birth and old age: of him I say this."

They are "peaceful" (santo) because they have stilled passion (rāga); they are peaceful because they have stilled hatred (dosa)… delusion (moha)… anger (kodha)… resentment (upanāha)… disparagement (makkha)… all unwholesome volitional formations (sabba-akusala-abhisankhāra).

Because they have been stilled, calmed, pacified, extinguished, quenched, departed, and tranquillized, they are called "peaceful," "calmed," "pacified," "quenched," and "tranquillized. Thus they are "peaceful."
"Smokeless" means that bodily misconduct has been shaken off, dispelled, dried up, withered away, and brought to an end;
verbal misconduct … mental misconduct has been shaken off, dispelled, dried up, withered away, and brought to an end;
lust … hatred … delusion has been shaken off, dispelled, dried up, withered away, and brought to an end; anger … resentment … hypocrisy … spite … [and so forth].
… envy … stinginess … deceit … guile … obstinacy … aggression … conceit … arrogance … intoxication … negligence … all defilements,
all misconducts, all distresses, all fevers, all torments, and all unwholesome volitional formations have been shaken off,
dispelled, dried up, completely withered away, and brought to an end.
Or alternatively, anger is called smoke:
"For pride, O Brahmin, is your burden of a bushel;
anger is the smoke, and lying is the ash."
The tongue is well-born, the heart is the seat of light;
the self well-tamed is the light of a man.
Moreover, anger arises in ten ways:
Anger arises thinking, "He has done me harm"; anger arises thinking, "He is doing me harm"; anger arises thinking, "He will do me harm.
Anger arises thinking, "He has done harm to one who is dear and pleasing to me," "He is doing harm to one who is dear and pleasing to me," or "He will do harm to one who is dear and pleasing to me.
[Conversely,] anger arises thinking, "He has done good to one who is not dear and not pleasing to me," "He is doing good to one who is not dear and not pleasing to me," or "He will do good..."
Anger arises thinking, "He will walk," or anger arises when there is no occasion for it.
Such as this is the mind’s irritation, resentment, hostility, opposition, vexation, provocation, intense provocation, hatred, malice, intense malice, the corruption of the mind,
mental corruption, anger, being angry, the state of being angry, hatred, being hateful, the state of being hateful.
Being corrupted, malice, being malicious, the state of being malicious, hostility, opposition, ferocity,
abruptness, and dissatisfaction of mind—
this is called anger.
Furthermore, the relative intensity of anger should be understood.
There is a time when anger merely causes turbidity of the mind, yet it does not yet cause the distortion of the facial features.
There is a time when anger merely causes the distortion of the facial features, yet it does not yet cause the clenching of the jaw.
At some times anger is merely enough to cause the gnashing of the jaws, yet one has not yet uttered harsh speech.
At some times anger is merely enough to utter harsh speech, yet one has not yet looked about in all directions.
At some times anger is merely enough to look about in all directions, yet one has not yet grasped a staff or a weapon.
At times, anger amounts merely to the grasping of a staff or a weapon, yet it does not yet amount to the brandishing of that staff or weapon.
At times, anger amounts merely to the brandishing of a staff or a weapon, yet it does not yet amount to the striking down of that staff or weapon.
At times, anger amounts merely to the striking down of a staff or a weapon, yet it does not yet amount to the cutting or tearing apart [of the victim].
At times anger is merely enough to cause a severing and breaking apart, yet it does not yet reach the point of crushing and shattering.
At times anger is merely enough to crush and shatter, yet it does not yet reach the point of tearing limb from limb.
At times anger is merely enough to tear limb from limb, yet it does not yet reach the point of depriving one of life.
At times, anger may amount merely to taking a life, yet it has not yet reached the point of being established in the relinquishment of everything.
When, however, after having caused another person to be killed, one kills oneself, to that extent anger has reached its highest peak and attained its greatest expansion.
One for whom that anger has been abandoned, cut off, stilled, subsided, rendered incapable of arising, and consumed by the fire of knowledge—he is called [a person who has transcended anger].

"Smokeless": because anger has been abandoned, it is smokeless; because the basis for anger has been fully understood, it is smokeless; because the cause of anger has been fully understood, it is smokeless; because the cause of anger has been cut off, it is smokeless. "Untroubled":
lust is trouble, hatred is trouble, delusion is trouble, anger is trouble, resentment is trouble... [and so on] ...all unwholesome volitional formations are trouble.
He for whom these afflictions have been abandoned, cut off, stilled, and calmed, rendered incapable of arising and consumed by the fire of knowledge—he is called "free from affliction" (*anīgha*).
"Free from longing" (*nirāsa*): "longing" (*āsā*) is said to be craving (*taṇhā*).
It is lust, infatuation... [as far as] covetousness, greed, the root of unwholesomeness.
He for whom this hope—that is, craving—has been abandoned, cut off, stilled, and calmed, rendered incapable of arising and burnt up by the fire of knowledge, is called "hopeless.
"Birth" refers to the birth, conception, descent, and manifestation of beings in their respective classes of beings; it is the appearance of the aggregates and the acquisition of the sense bases.

"Aging" refers to the aging and decrepitude of those respective beings in their respective classes of beings; it is the brokenness, graying of hair, wrinkling of skin, decline of the life-span, and maturation of the faculties.
"He who is peaceful, smokeless, untroubled, and free from longing has crossed over birth and aging—this is what I say. By this I mean:

he who is peaceful, smokeless, untroubled, and free from longing has crossed over, transcended, leaped over, surmounted, passed beyond, declared, explained, taught, established, revealed, analyzed, made plain, and elucidated birth, aging, and death—this is what I say, I declare, I teach, I prescribe, I set forth, I disclose, I analyze, I make clear, and I reveal.
The noble one is smokeless, free from distress, and desireless; he has crossed over birth and old age—this I declare.
Therefore the Blessed One said:
"Having discerned the higher and lower worlds in this world..."
"Puṇṇaka," said the Blessed One,
"he for whom there is no trembling anywhere in the world—
he who is peaceful, smokeless, free from distress, and without longing."
“He has crossed over birth and old age,” I say.
At the conclusion of this verse...
[he remained] sitting with palms joined, paying homage to the Blessed One.
“The Blessed One is my teacher, venerable sir; I am his disciple.
This concludes the third exposition: the Questions of the Young Man Puṇṇaka.
